doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: San Francisco's healthy, world-music jazz scene
summary: Marshall describes a healthy San Francisco jazz climate, young players returning from East Coast schools, and jazz blending with local ethnic musics from Basque to West African.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: A very healthy music climate here. I feel a very healthy jazz climate. This isn’t the jazz center of the world but a lot of these young musicians, who some of them I had the pleasure of teaching and they’ve gone off to schools like the New School in New York and Berklee School of Music, a lot the East Coast schools, they’ve come back to San Francisco and they are working all over the place. And they are very fine musicians. It’s not like a jazz mecca, it’s more like a world music mecca if anything, in this area.
Yeah. When I look in the newspapers I see a lot of different kinds of things happening. You have an Asian community here obviously that adds its own flavor.

It’s own flavor, yep, to the jazz music. It is quite amazing how these people from different backgrounds and different ethnic persuasions with their own musical history and how jazz music just fits in with all of these different musics. I just got back from Spain about a month or so ago. I was in the Basque country, and I hear this music, and I can’t even pronounce the gentleman’s name, but there was music that was Basque folk songs but played in the flavor of like Weather Report or something like that. And it was just amazing. And all over the world it’s like that. You go to West Africa, that’s a big example, you know the harmonies, it’s no more like the African really simple chords and they’re just like full blown modern, contemporary musicians playing a jazz version of their ethnic music, and just really killing it. I mean I’m sort of like dismayed at the music — I can’t even call it a phenomenon — but the music trend that’s going on now with the © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

hip hop music. And it’s not to put down a music, because I don’t believe there’s any music there to put down. The concern I have is that these children, there is a generation of children in America, not just black kids but children in general, growing up without hearing a melody or a chord, or even a lyric.
